title: Patterns in Times Tables
keyIdea: The multiplication square is full of patterns, and each one has a reason. An answer is odd only when both factors are odd; one even factor makes it even. The square is symmetric about its diagonal because a × b = b × a. Two rows add to make another row: 2 × 7 + 4 × 7 = 6 × 7, because 2 sevens and 4 sevens make 6 sevens. In the 9s, 9 × n is 10 × n take away n, so the tens go up, the ones go down and, up to 9 × 10, the digits add to 9. A pattern is only true if no answer breaks it: the 3s are not all odd, because 3 × 2 = 6.
familyTip: Draw a 10 by 10 times table square together. Colour every odd answer, then ask your child why the odd answers only sit where the row and the column are both odd. Fold the paper along the diagonal and check the matching answers.

visual.caption: Is the answer even or odd? Drag each fact to a box, or tap the fact and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: on a 10 × 10 times square, sort even and odd answers, fold on the diagonal, add rows, fill the 9s and test claims.

kid: In a times table square, each answer is a row number times a column number. Colour the odd answers. They only show up where the row and the column are both odd. 7 × 9 = 63 is odd. 7 × 6 = 42 is even, because 6 is even.
Fold the square from corner to corner. 3 × 8 lands on 8 × 3, and both are 24. You can swap the two numbers and get the same answer.
Rows add up. 2 sevens and 4 sevens make 6 sevens. So 2 × 7 + 4 × 7 = 6 × 7. That is 14 + 28 = 42.
Look at the 9s: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45. The tens go up by 1 and the ones go down by 1. The digits add to 9. That is because 9 × 4 is 10 fours take away one 4: 40 − 4 = 36.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. US Common Core 3.OA.D.9 asks pupils to identify arithmetic patterns, including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table, and explain them using properties of operations, for example that 4 times a number is always even. The National Curriculum for England expects recall of multiplication facts to 12 × 12 by the end of Year 4, and the non-statutory guidance stresses using commutativity and known facts to derive new ones.

Each pattern here has a reason that pupils can say. Odd × odd = odd, and any even factor gives an even product. The square is symmetric about its leading diagonal because multiplication is commutative. Adding two rows gives a third, because a × n + b × n = (a + b) × n, which is the distributive property. The 9s follow from 9 × n = 10 × n − n. A claim such as every 3s answer is odd is tested by looking for one counterexample.

Common mistakes: thinking 7 × 6 is odd because 7 is odd; treating 6 × 8 and 8 × 6 as two facts to learn; adding the row numbers wrongly or multiplying them (row 3 and row 4 make row 7, not row 12); in the 9s, writing 10 × n instead of 9 × n or a number such as 74 whose digits do not add to 9; and accepting a pattern from a few cases without checking the whole row. In the lab each slip gets a message that names the fact that breaks it.

practice.hint: Is one of the factors even? What do 7 lots of an even number make?
practice.explain: 6 is even, so 7 × 6 = 42 is even. An answer is odd only when both factors are odd.

practice.prompt: 2 × {n} + 4 × {n} is the same as 6 × {n}. What is it?
practice.hint: Work out 2 × {n} and 4 × {n}, then add. Or find 6 × {n} straight away.
practice.explain: 2 × {n} + 4 × {n} = {=2*n} + {=4*n} = {=6*n}. Two lots and four lots make six lots: 6 × {n} = {=6*n}.

practice.hint: 9 lots of {n} is one {n} less than 10 lots of {n}.

practice.prompt: Which fact has the same answer as 3 × 8?
practice.hint: Swap the order of the two numbers.
practice.explain: 8 × 3 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24. On the square they sit opposite each other across the diagonal.

practice.prompt: Ben says every answer in the 3 times table is odd. Is he right?
practice.hint: Try 3 × 2. One answer that breaks the claim is enough.
practice.explain: 3 × 2 = 6 is even, so the claim is false. The 3s go odd, even, odd, even: 3, 6, 9, 12.

pool.hint: An answer is odd only when both factors are odd.
pool.explain: 5 and 9 are both odd, so 5 × 9 = 45 is odd. 5 × 8 = 40 and 4 × 9 = 36 each have an even factor.

pool.prompt: Row 3 + row 4 of the square makes which row?
pool.hint: 3 lots and 4 lots make how many lots?
pool.explain: 3 lots + 4 lots = 7 lots, so row 3 + row 4 = row 7. For example 3 × 5 + 4 × 5 = 15 + 20 = 35 = 7 × 5.

pool.prompt: Which number is in the 9 times table?
pool.hint: Up to 9 × 10, the digits of a 9s answer add to 9.
pool.explain: 8 + 1 = 9 and 81 = 9 × 9. 84 has digits adding to 12, and 99 is 9 × 11, beyond the 10 × 10 square.

pool.hint: 10 is 5 + 5, so the 10s answer is double the 5s answer.

pool.prompt: Why is every answer in the 4 times table even?
choices: 4 is 2 × 2, so each answer is a double
pool.explain: 4 × n = 2 × (2 × n), and 2 times any whole number is even. 4 × 3 = 12 is even.
54 + 9 = 63. The tens go up by 1 and the ones go down by 1. 64 adds 10, and 56 is 7 × 8.

pool.hint: 3 lots and 5 lots make 8 lots. Add the two answers.

pool.prompt: On the square, which cell is the mirror of row 2, column 9 across the diagonal?
pool.hint: The fold swaps the row and the column.
pool.explain: Row 9, column 2 is 9 × 2 = 18, the same as 2 × 9. Row 3, column 6 is also 18, but it is a different fact, not the mirror.
